Abstract
This paper tacklesopen-ended deep research (OEDR), a complex challenge
where AI agents must synthesize vast web-scale information into insightful re-
ports. Current approaches are plagued by dual-fold limitations: static research
pipelines that decouple planning from evidence acquisition and monolithic
generation paradigms that include redundant, irrelevant evidence, suffering
from hallucination issues and low citation accuracy. To address these chal-
lenges, we introduceWebWeaver, a novel dual-agent framework that emulates
the human research process. The planner operates in a dynamic cycle, itera-
tively interleaving evidence acquisition with outline optimization to produce
a comprehensive, citation-grounded outline linking to a memory bank of evi-
dence. The writer then executes a hierarchical retrieval and writing process,
composing the report section by section. By performing targeted retrieval of
only the necessary evidence from the memory bank via citations for each part,
it effectively mitigates long-context issues and citation hallucinations. Our
framework establishes a new state-of-the-art across major OEDR benchmarks,
including DeepResearch Bench, DeepConsult, and DeepResearchGym. These
results validate our human-centric, iterative methodology, demonstrating that
adaptive planning and focused synthesis are crucial for producing comprehen-
sive, trusted, and well-structured reports.

by feeding all the evidence into LLMs. In contrast, our approach uniquely enables the outline to be
dynamically optimized in tandem with the evidence acquisition process, allowing for a comprehensive,
source-grounded research outline. While recent works (Huot et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024) adopted the
multi-agent paradigm to write sections in parallel, with evidence retrieval based on the section title,
the separate writing often leads to content and style incoherence, and the retrieval using titles also
brings noisy evidence. In contrast, our agentic hierarchical writing model is designed to foster both
global coherence and local depth. Its sequential, single-agent process allows cross-sectional thinking
by maintaining a continuous narrative flow between sections. At the same time, its reliance on precise,
citation-grounded evidence enables deep internal reasoning within each section. This combination allows
the writer to produce a cohesive, accurate, and insightful report.
6 Conclusion
In this paper, we introduced WebWeaver, a novel dual-agent framework designed to overcome the
fundamental flaws of static, machine-like pipelines in open-ended deep research (OEDR). By emulating
the human cognitive process that integrates the planner’s dynamic research cycle with the writer’s

hierarchical retrieval and writing process, WebWeaver consistently outperforms both proprietary and
open-source systems, establishing a new state-of-the-art.
Beyond its superior performance, the true significance of WebWeaver lies in the new paradigm it offers
the community for tackling complex, information-intensive tasks. It reframes the intractable challenge of
long-context reasoning, demonstrating that it can be successfully deconstructed into a structured problem
of system-level information management, orchestrated through a series of precise actions. Both the
planner and writer are embodiments of this principle: they use tools to dynamically explore, structure,
and write, rather than passively processing it in a single pass. This work does not just present a better
agent system; it presents a new blueprint for building the agent system that masters intensive knowledge
through deliberate actions, not just brute-force attention.

article.body:
Consider a chef who tastes a dish mid-recipe to decide whether to add more salt or start over entirely. As an analogy, computer workers examine how artificial systems monitor their own choices during complex tasks. Our group is investigating how these systems allocate their mental effort between planning and execution. [1]

Team members 100, 101, 102, and 103 analyzed how reasoning models handle external oversight and multi-turn problems. Their recorded readings indicate that metareasoning governs how resources are split between planning and action. Paper-supported notes suggest that multi-turn models show distinct behavioral shifts under external supervision, while autonomous frameworks require self-generated goals to acquire flexible skills. [1, 2, 3, 4]

Meanwhile, teams 200, 201, 202, and 203 looked into epistemic self-correction and preference formation. Their findings highlight that inferential errors during preference updates are often path-dependent under misspecified models. Furthermore, recorded reviews emphasize that intrinsic self-correction remains fundamentally limited without external validation signals. [5, 6, 7, 8]

Rounding out the group, teams 300, 301, 302, and 303 explored curiosity-driven learning and multi-agent coordination. Their notebook records note that curiosity-driven strategies help agents explore complex problems with rare rewards, while structured communication dimensions improve joint performance across multiple units. [9, 10, 11, 12]

How can explicit falsification mechanisms be generalized across more diverse, unconstrained scientific domains when intrinsic correction falls short? [5]

Summary

We study how computer systems examine their reasoning using published papers. We look at resource management, preferences, and self-correction limits. We still do not know if systems can truly question their starting rules. We follow the Console as new readings arrive.
article.lede: We continue exploring how computer systems examine their own reasoning, tracking the shift from rigid calculations to flexible self-evaluation.
article.lens: Investigating the boundaries of automated reflection through shared source readings and safety frameworks.
article.title: Mapping the Machinery of Machine Reflection
